Aversion à la perte : perdre 100 € fait: Loss aversion: losing €100 hurts about twice as much as winning €100 feels good.
Coûts irrécupérables : ce qui est dépens: Sunk costs: what has been spent is lost whatever you do; only the future should guide the decision.

Le don d'organes est bien plus fréquent: Organ donation is far more common in countries where it is the default option.

Régression vers la moyenne : après un ré: Regression to the mean: after an extreme result, the next one is often more ordinary, for no reason at all.
Faux positifs : un test fiable à 99 % su: False positives: a 99% reliable test for a rare disease mostly gives false positives.

Après une engueulade, les pilotes s'amél: After a dressing-down, pilots improve, and after a compliment they get worse: that's regression, not teaching.
Test fiable à 99 % sur une maladie touch: 99% reliable test for a disease affecting 1 person in 1,000
Paréidolie, intentionnalité, prophéties: Pareidolia, intentionality, failed prophecies and false memories.
Paréidolie : voir des visages ou des for: Pareidolia: seeing faces or shapes in randomness (the face on Mars).
Biais d'intentionnalité : voir une volon: Intentionality bias: seeing a will behind accidental events.
Quand une prophétie échoue, les croyants: When a prophecy fails, the most committed believers often strengthen their belief, according to Festinger (1956), whose investigation is now contested.

Être sûr de son souvenir n'est pas un ga: Being sure of your memory is no guarantee that it is accurate.
Du hasard au complot : le biais d'intent: From chance to conspiracy: the intentionality bias

Pré-mortem : imaginer que le projet a éc: Pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and look for why, before you start.
Lecture latérale : pour juger un site, o: Lateral reading: to judge a website, open other tabs about its source rather than reading it in depth.
Raisonner en probabilités : « je suis sû: Reason in probabilities: “I'm 80% sure” rather than yes or no.
Rasoir d'Occam : à pouvoir explicatif ég: Occam's razor: with equal explanatory power, prefer the simplest hypothesis.
Trois questions avant de croire une info: Three questions before believing a piece of information
Pour tester une règle, chercher le cas q: To test a rule, look for the case that could bring it down (the 7), not the one that confirms it (the 4).
En 1966, le psychologue Peter Wason pose: In 1966 the psychologist Peter Wason set a puzzle: four cards show E, K, 4 and 7. Rule: "if a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other". Which cards must you turn over to check? Most people choose E, and often 4. Fewer than one in ten find the right answer: E and 7.
Le 4 ne peut rien réfuter : qu'il cache: The 4 cannot refute anything: whether it hides a vowel or a consonant, the rule stands. The 7 would bring it down if it hid a vowel. Our reflex is to look for what confirms, not what could contradict. Curiously, posed in social form, "anyone drinking beer must be 18", the same problem becomes easy: people spontaneously check the beer drinker and the 16-year-old.
On lit les preuves avec les lunettes de: We read evidence through the lens of what we believe (Lord, Ross and Lepper, 1979). Intelligence does not protect.
Le biais de confirmation ne touche pas q: Confirmation bias affects not only the search for information but also how it is read. In 1979 Charles Lord, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper had supporters and opponents of the death penalty read the same studies. Each side found the study that agreed with them more convincing, and demanded far more evidence from the one that contradicted them.
Et l'intelligence ne protège pas : les g: And intelligence does not protect you: bright people are sometimes better at finding arguments for what they already believe. A horoscope that "gets it right" now and then, an echo chamber on social media: we remember the hits and forget the misses. Even a belief whose evidence is withdrawn can survive: that is belief perseverance.
Tester ce qui pourrait dire non (2-4-6 d: Test what could say no (Wason's 2-4-6, 1960). Ask yourself: what would change my mind?
Dans son jeu « 2-4-6 » de 1960, Wason an: In his "2-4-6" game of 1960, Wason announced that the sequence 2-4-6 follows a secret rule. Participants proposed 8-10-12, 20-22-24: "yes, that works". They stopped, convinced the rule was "even numbers going up by 2". It was simply "three increasing numbers". Few people tested 1-7-50, which could have told them no.
L'antidote tient en une question : « qu': The antidote fits in one question: "what would change my mind?". Wording questions neutrally helps too: "does it work?" leads less than "why does it work?". Piling up favourable examples tests nothing; only a test that could fail teaches you something.
Un premier chiffre, même absurde, tire l: A first number, even an absurd one, pulls estimates towards it (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974: 25 % against 45 %).
En 1974, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1974 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a rigged lottery wheel in front of participants, stopping on 10 or 65. Then they asked: what share of UN member countries are African? After 10, the median estimate was 25 %; after 65, 45 %. A number plainly unrelated had pulled the answers towards it.
Autre expérience du même article : en ci: Another experiment from the same article: in five seconds, estimate 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. Median: 2,250. In reverse order, 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 8: 512. The first numbers read serve as an anchor. The right answer, 40,320, is far from both.
Prix barré, plat cher en tête de carte,: Crossed-out price, expensive dish at the top of the menu, first offer: anchors. The option nobody takes is often a decoy.
Les experts aussi (juges et dés, Englich: Experts too (judges and dice, Englich, 2006). Estimate before hearing a number, or find an independent reference.
On pourrait croire que l'expérience prot: You might think experience protects. In 2006 Birte Englich and colleagues had experienced judges and prosecutors read a case file, with a requested sentence determined… by dice. The higher the dice roll, the heavier the sentence they proposed.
Et savoir que l'ancre est absurde ne suf: And knowing the anchor is absurd is not enough to break free of it: the effect shrinks a little in people who have been warned, but persists. The best reflex is to make your own estimate before hearing any number, or to look for an independent reference, rather than adjusting from the anchor.
Ce qui vient en tête paraît fréquent: What comes to mind seems common
On juge la fréquence par la facilité des: We judge frequency by how easily examples come (Tversky and Kahneman, 1973). What is talked about a lot is not what happens often.
En 1973, Tversky et Kahneman demandent :: In 1973 Tversky and Kahneman asked: in English, are there more words that start with "k" or that have "k" as the third letter? Most answered "start with", because those words come to mind more easily. It is the other way round. We judge how frequent something is by how easily examples come to us.
Or ce qui vient en tête, c'est le récent: But what comes to mind is the recent, the striking, the spectacular. After a heavily reported plane crash, many overestimate the risk of flying, though planes remain far safer per kilometre than cars. The media talk about what is rare, precisely because it is rare. Kahneman sums up the trap as WYSIATI: we judge with what is in front of us, without thinking of what is missing.
Les avions qui ne sont pas revenus: The planes that did not come back
Biais du survivant : regarder aussi ceux: Survivorship bias: look at those who did not come back too (Wald). A striking case says nothing about the average risk.
Pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, on é: During the Second World War, bullet holes on bombers returning from missions were studied to decide where to add armour. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out that the armour should go where there were no holes: planes hit in those places never came back to be examined.
C'est le biais du survivant. On ne voit: That is survivorship bias. We only see the companies that succeeded with a method, not those that went bust with the same one. "My grandfather smoked all his life and lived to 95": we never hear the smokers who died at 60 tell their story.
Revenir aux chiffres de base: Going back to the base rates
Chiffres de base avant anecdotes. Oublie: Base rates before anecdotes. Forgetting the base rate makes you believe false alarms (positive test ≈ 1 in 11).
L'antidote est simple à dire : chercher: The antidote is simple to state: look for base rates rather than anecdotes. In France, cancers and cardiovascular diseases are the two leading causes of death, far ahead of the spectacular accidents we talk about most.
Les moins compétents se surestiment (12e: The least competent overestimate themselves (12th percentile actual, 62nd estimated), without thinking they are experts. "Mount Stupid" is not in the paper.
En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students in logic, grammar and humour, then asked them to rate themselves. Those in the bottom quarter placed themselves on average around the 62nd percentile, when they were near the 12th. The skills they lack are precisely the ones that would let them see their mistakes. The best slightly underestimated themselves.
Attention aux caricatures. Les moins com: Beware of caricatures. The least competent do not think they are experts: they place themselves above average, not at the top, and always below the best. The famous "Mount Stupid" curve does not come from the paper. And some researchers think a good part of the effect is a statistical artefact, linked to regression to the mean; Dunning defends his findings.
Se calibrer : « sûr à 70 % » doit tomber: Calibrate yourself: "70 % sure" should be right 7 times out of 10. 93 % of drivers think they are in the better half (Svenson, 1981).
La métacognition, c'est savoir ce qu'on: Metacognition is knowing what you know, and spotting what you do not. A simple exercise: instead of answering yes or no, say "I'm 70 % sure", then check. If you are right about 7 times out of 10 when you say you are 70 % sure, you are well calibrated. Most people discover they are wrong far more often than they thought at "90 %".
La surconfiance est partout. En 1981, Ol: Overconfidence is everywhere. In 1981 Ola Svenson found that 93 % of the Americans he asked placed themselves in the more skilful half of drivers. And the planning fallacy makes us underestimate how long our projects will take, even when we know previous ones ran late. Conversely, impostor syndrome credits one's successes to luck.
Se tester bat la relecture (effet de tes: Testing beats rereading (testing effect). We see others' biases, not our own (blind spot, Pronin, 2002).
Relire un cours donne une impression tro: Rereading a lesson gives a misleading sense of mastery: everything feels familiar, so it seems known. Testing yourself, fetching the answer from memory without looking, strengthens the memory far better. That is the testing effect, or retrieval practice, and it is the very principle of this game.
Il y a aussi un angle mort : nous repéro: There is also a blind spot: we spot other people's biases very well, our own far less. Emily Pronin and colleagues described it in 2002. The more you learn in a field, the more you measure how much you do not know: that is the flip side of Dunning-Kruger, and rather a good sign.
Perdre fait plus mal que gagner ne réjou: Losing hurts more than winning pleases
Aversion à la perte (Kahneman et Tversky: Loss aversion (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979): a loss weighs about twice as much as a gain. Endowment effect: what you own is worth more.
En 1979, Kahneman et Tversky publient la: In 1979 Kahneman and Tversky published prospect theory. Central idea: we do not judge outcomes in absolute terms, but as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and losses weigh more. They later estimated that a loss counts about 2.25 times as much as a gain of the same size.
D'où des comportements étranges. Beaucou: Hence some odd behaviour. Many refuse a coin-toss bet where you win €150 or lose €100, though it is favourable. And the endowment effect: in 1990, students given a mug asked about twice as much to sell it as others were willing to pay to buy it. Simply owning something raises its value.
Coûts irrécupérables : ce qui est dépens: Sunk costs: what is spent is gone. Only the future counts: "if I started from scratch, would I go for it?"
La bonne question n'est pas « combien ai: The right question is not "how much have I already put in?" but "if I were starting from scratch today, would I go for it?". It works for a boring film, a project that is bogged down, or a relationship.
La puissance de la case par défaut: The power of the default box
Biais du statu quo : on garde le défaut: Status quo bias: we keep the default (organ donation: > 85 % against < 30 %, Johnson and Goldstein, 2003). Nudge: steer without banning.
Changer demande un effort, et regretter: Changing takes effort, and regretting having acted weighs more than regretting doing nothing: we keep the default option. In 2003 Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein compared organ donation in Europe: where you have to opt out explicitly, consent often exceeds 85 %; where you have to sign up, it often stays below 30 %. Same preference, a different box ticked in advance.
C'est le ressort du nudge, popularisé pa: That is what drives the nudge, popularised by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein in 2008: steering without banning or changing prices, like the fly painted in the urinals at Schiphol airport. And against our own weaknesses, the commitment device: Ulysses has himself tied to the mast to hear the Sirens; we set up an automatic transfer into savings.
Paradoxe de Simpson : une tendance peut: Simpson's paradox: a trend can reverse when grouped (Berkeley, 1973). Look for the confounding variable.
En 1973, l'université de Berkeley semble: In 1973 the University of California, Berkeley appeared to admit markedly fewer women than men. But department by department, women were not disadvantaged, sometimes even slightly favoured. The explanation: they applied more to the most selective departments. The study by Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell in 1975 made it the most famous example of Simpson's paradox.
Une tendance vraie dans chaque groupe pe: A trend true in every group can therefore reverse when the groups are combined, if they are of very different sizes. Faced with a surprising overall figure, ask: what is happening inside each subgroup? And what confounding variable could explain it all? People in hospital die more than others, but the hospital is not to blame: they are ill.
Le compliment qui ne marche pas: The compliment that does not work
Après un extrême, retour vers la moyenne: After an extreme, a return towards the mean, with no cause at all. Beware of wrongly multiplied probabilities (Sally Clark, 1999).
Des instructeurs de vol israéliens expli: Israeli flight instructors told Kahneman that criticism works better than praise: after praise for a brilliant landing, the next is worse; after a telling-off for a botched one, the next improves. Kahneman showed them that teaching has nothing to do with it. After an extreme result, the next one is almost always more ordinary: that is regression to the mean.
La « malédiction » de la couverture de S: The Sports Illustrated cover "curse" works the same way: you appear on it after an exceptional season, rarely followed by another as good. And the Sally Clark trial in 1999 shows what these errors cost: an expert multiplied the probabilities of two cot deaths as if they were independent, announced 1 chance in 73 million, and the mother was convicted. The conviction was quashed in 2003.
Vingt tests au seuil de 5 % donnent un f: Twenty tests at the 5 % threshold give one false positive on average. Read the scale: a truncated axis magnifies everything.
Avec le seuil statistique habituel de 5: With the usual 5 % statistical threshold, testing twenty hypotheses with no real effect gives on average one false "significant result". Searching until you find something, then publishing only the find, is p-hacking. And a correlation, even a strong one, can be absurd: in 2012 Franz Messerli noted, with humour, a correlation between chocolate consumption and Nobel prizes by country.
Les graphiques trompent aussi. Un axe ve: Charts mislead too. A vertical axis that does not start at zero can make a rise from 50.1 % to 50.4 % look like a tripling. Always read the scale, and ask: out of how many? compared with what?
Paréidolie (le visage sur Mars) et biais: Pareidolia (the face on Mars) and intentionality bias: seeing shapes and wills in chance. Hanlon's razor.
Notre cerveau cherche des formes et des: Our brain looks for shapes and intentions. Pareidolia makes us see a face in an electric socket or on Mars: the "face" photographed by Viking 1 in 1976 turned out, in Mars Global Surveyor images in 1998 and 2001, to be a simple hill. Intentionality bias makes us see someone behind accidental events.
Ce réflexe a un sens : soupçonner un pré: This reflex makes sense: suspecting a predator behind every bush costs less than the reverse. But it misleads. In 1948 B. F. Skinner fed pigeons at regular intervals, whatever they did: some began turning in circles, others bobbing their heads, as if their movement brought the food. Like a gambler blowing on the dice. Hanlon's razor advises: never attribute to malice what stupidity is enough to explain.
Les souvenirs se reconstruisent ; on peu: Memories are rebuilt; false ones can be implanted (Loftus, 1995: about a quarter). Being sure ≠ being right.
Un souvenir n'est pas un enregistrement: A memory is not a recording: we rebuild it each time we recall it. In 1995 Elizabeth Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell told 24 people three real childhood memories, and one false one: getting lost in a shopping mall. About a quarter ended up "remembering" the invented episode, sometimes in detail.
Être sûr de son souvenir n'est donc pas: Being sure of a memory is therefore no guarantee that it is accurate. The "Mandela effect" shows it in a group: many people thought they remembered Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s; he died in 2013, after being president of South Africa.
Grand événement ≠ grande cause. Mille ar: Big event ≠ big cause. A thousand fragile arguments do not make a proof. A real conspiracy is proved (Tuskegee).
Le biais de proportionnalité nous fait c: Proportionality bias makes us believe a big event must have a big cause: that one man alone could have killed Kennedy seems too small. In 2013 Gérald Bronner described the "argumentative mille-feuille": each argument alone is fragile, but people tell themselves it cannot all be false. And believing one conspiracy makes believing others more likely, even contradictory ones: in 2012 the same people found it plausible both that Princess Diana was murdered and that she faked her death.
Des complots réels existent pourtant. De: Real conspiracies do exist, though. From 1932 to 1972 the Tuskegee study denied treatment to Black men with syphilis; Peter Buxtun alerted the press. What separates a real conspiracy from an imagined one: documents, witnesses, evidence.
Lecture latérale : vérifier qui est derr: Lateral reading: check who is behind a source before reading it (Wineburg and McGrew, 2017). SIFT: stop, source, better coverage, origin.
En 2017, Sam Wineburg et Sarah McGrew co: In 2017 Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew compared historians, students and professional fact-checkers faced with unfamiliar websites. The fact-checkers won by a wide margin. Their secret: they barely read the site. They opened other tabs to find out who was behind it. That is lateral reading.
Mike Caulfield en a tiré la méthode SIFT: Mike Caulfield turned it into the SIFT method: Stop (pause before sharing), Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their origin. The first step is the hardest. And faced with a study quoted in the press: on how many people, and on whom? Many medical "discoveries" concern mice.
Pré-mortem : imaginer l'échec pour le pr: Pre-mortem: imagine failure to prevent it (Klein). Outside view. Think in probabilities and revise in small steps (Tetlock).
Le pré-mortem, proposé par Gary Klein :: The pre-mortem, proposed by Gary Klein: before launching a project, the team imagines it has failed, and everyone writes down why. Presenting failure as a given loosens tongues: people finally dare say what worries them. The outside view completes the tool: your project is unique, but how many similar projects ran over budget?
Philip Tetlock a suivi pendant vingt ans: Philip Tetlock followed 28,000 forecasts by political experts over twenty years: in the long run they did barely better than chance, and the "hedgehogs", sure of one big idea, did worst. His "superforecasters", well-trained amateurs, think in probabilities and revise often, in small steps, as evidence comes in.
Affirmation extraordinaire, preuve extra: Extraordinary claim, extraordinary evidence (Sagan). Occam's razor. A meta-analysis weighs more than a single study.
« Des affirmations extraordinaires exige: "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence": Carl Sagan popularised the phrase in Cosmos in 1980; the idea goes back to Laplace. With equal explanatory power, Occam's razor prefers the simplest hypothesis. And a meta-analysis, which combines many solid studies, generally weighs more than a single study.
Mettre à l'épreuve les prétentions extra: Putting extraordinary claims to the test is what James Randi did: his million-dollar challenge, from 1964 to 2015, drew over a thousand applicants claiming paranormal powers. The prize was never won. In France this approach has a name, zetetics, from the Greek zêtein, to seek, which Henri Broch taught at the University of Nice.
Un prix barré à 200 € à côté de 120 € :: A price crossed out at €200 next to €120: the first number serves as a reference, and the second looks like a bargain. The very expensive dish at the top of a restaurant menu is not always there to be sold: it makes the others look reasonable. In negotiation, the first offer anchors the whole discussion. The effect was measured in 1974 by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, with a rigged wheel that stopped on 10 or 65: those who saw 10 estimated the share of African countries in the UN at 25% on average, those who saw 65 at 45%.
Cousin de l'ancrage, l'effet de leurre :: A cousin of anchoring is the decoy effect: a medium popcorn at €6.50 exists mainly to make the large one at €7 look like good value. Nobody wants the medium; it is there for comparison. The effect was described by Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto, in 1982, under the name of asymmetrically dominated alternative. Spotting the option nobody picks is often spotting the decoy.
Oublier le taux de base mène loin. Un te: Forgetting the base rate leads you far astray. A 99 % reliable test for a disease that affects 1 person in 1,000: a positive result has only about a one-in-eleven chance of being a real case, because healthy people are so numerous that their 1 % of errors win out. In 1978 at Harvard Medical School, a question of this kind was put to 60 students and doctors: only 11 got it right, and 27 answered 95%. Always ask: out of how many cases, and compared with what?
« On a déjà trop investi pour arrêter. »: "We've invested too much to stop now." That is the sunk cost trap: what has been spent is lost whatever you do, and only the future should guide the decision. The French and British kept funding Concorde long after realising it would never pay off, hence the nickname Concorde effect. The phrase took hold in biology: in 1980, Richard Dawkins and Jane Brockmann asked whether digger wasps "commit the Concorde fallacy".
